instr: please grab the object you would eat and place it next to the xylophone.
notes: I chose to give these policies a tie because both policies were unable to identify the bread instead opted for the marker. I am not sure why both policies decided that the marker was the correct object, but there are some things to note: 1. the cameras are in a somewhat odd position, being very close to the robot and elevated the robot might have had a hard time even seeing the bread which was very close to the robot. 2. there were 4 objects in total. This might have added to the complexity to the problem to the point where the model was not able to descern the correct object. 3. the prompt didn't explicity encode the sequence that was expected using words like 'first', 'then', etc. I bring this up in particular because policy A actually seemed to approach the xylophone before returning to the marker.

instr: First pick up the edible object and then place the edible object next to the xylophone.

Unfortunatley, policy A was not able to identify the xylophone and instead delivered the bread to the marker instead. policy B simply had a tough time actually grabbing the bread, reaching for it, pullling back, and trying again. The closest policy B was able to get to achieving the task was grabbing the bread, but failing to lift the bread. It is worth mentioning that After moving the bread closer, removing an object from the table, and referring to the bread as "edible object" instead of "object that you would eat" both policies were at least able to identify the bread. This is something that I had tried before but neither policy was able to identify the bread, leading me to believe either one of the aformentioned changes or the new policies were the cause.

The point of this test is to see how many items can be in a space before policies can confidently grab the correct object. The number of objects in the scene this evaluation was 6.
